These criminal appeals are preferred by the accused appellants Kapil, Harishchand, Gopi, Veerpal,
Ratan Pal, Kamlesh, Tejvir, Sachin and Vikki challenging the judgment and order dated 13.02.2019,
passed by the Additional Sessions Judge/Fast Track Court No. 01, Meerut in Sessions Trial No.1190 of 2016 (State Vs. Kapil and others) and Sessions Trial No. 1191 of 2016 (State Vs. Sachin and another), arising out of Case Crime No. 74 of 2016, under Sections 498A, 201, 304B, alternative Section 302/149 and 3/4 Dowry Prohibition Act, Police Station-Ganganagar, District - Meerut,
whereby the appellants Kapil, Ratan Pal, Kamlesh, Tejvir, Sachin and Vikki have been sentenced to rigorous life imprisonment along with fine of Rs.20,000/- under Section 302 r/w 149 IPC and in default of payment of fine to undergo one year additional imprisonment.

The appellants Kapil,
Ratan Pal, Kamlesh, Tejvir, Sachin, Vikki, Gopi, Harishchand and Veerpal have been sentenced to three years six months rigorous imprisonment along with fine of Rs.3,000/- under Section 201/511 IPC and in default of payment of fine to undergo one month additional imprisonment.
All the sentences are directed to run concurrently.
2. Accused persons are the husband and in-laws of the deceased who died on 24th March, 2016.
Father of the deceased has made a written report saying that he had married his daughter to the accused Kapil as per Hindu Rites and Rituals on 18th April, 2012.
He had also given dowry as per his financial capability.
The husband and other relatives however were not happy with the dowry and used to harass his daughter and also beat her from time to time.
Two months prior to the incident a sum of Rs. 1 lac was demanded by the accused persons and she was also harassed to secure dowry.
On 24th March, 2016 the mother-in-law of the deceased telephonically informed that the deceased has fallen sick.
The informant instructed his brother-in-law (sala) Vinod and brother-in-law (behnoi) Shaudan to come to Rajpura where his daughter was married.
By the time these persons reached they saw that the deceased was taken to the burning ghat and she was being cremated.
After seeing these relatives the accused persons fled from the place of occurrence.

2 the help of others the two relatives Vinod and Shaudan doused the fire.
Shaudan and Vinod then informed of the incident to the informant who came to the burning ghat and saw that half burnt body of the deceased had already been taken out of the pyre.
It was alleged that with the intent to suppress evidence the body was being cremated by the accused persons.

With these allegations the first information report came to be lodged in the matter as Case Crime No.74 of 2016, under Sections 304B, 498A, 201 IPC and 3/4 Dowry Prohibition Act at 2.00 pm on 24.3.2016.

The written report is exhibited as Exhibit Ka-1.
3.
Investigation proceeded in the matter and the burnt ashes as well as broken bangles and other articles worn by the deceased were taken in possession vide Exhibit Ka-14 to Ka-15.
The inquest was conducted at 2.30 pm on 24.3.2016.
The inquest witnesses opined that postmortem be conducted to ascertain the cause of death.
The body was sealed and thereafter sent to mortuary for conducting postmortem.

The postmortem was conducted on the next day i.e. 25.3.2016, wherein following postmortem burn injuries were found on the deceased:
"(i) severely burnt body is received and chhared.
(ii) Burst wound present over the left side of skull.
(iii) Superficial to deep burn present whole body.
(iv) part of foot below ankle is missing due to burn and chhared.
(v) both lower limb tied with the help of rope at the level of thigh.
(vi) rarely air filled vesicle found (vii) no redness and erthyma over around the burn area.
(viii) In trachea no froth and carbon particles present."
4. Viscera was preserved and sent to Forensic Science Laboratory, Agra, U.P. for examination.
The report in that regard, dated 6.5.2017, is on record.

The investigation proceeded in the matter and ultimately a charge sheet came to be submitted against the accused appellants Kapil, Ratan Pal,
Kamlesh and Tejvir under Sections 498A/201/304B IPC read with 3/4 Dowry Prohibition Act.
Alternative charge was framed under Section 302/149 IPC.
The accused persons were explained the charges, who denied their implication and demanded trial.
Charges were also framed against accused Gopi, Harishchand and Veerpal under Section 201 IPC.
They too denied charges and demanded trial.
Charges were also framed against accused Sachin and Vikki under Section 201 IPC r/w 498A/304B IPC and 3/4 Dowry Prohibition Act and alternative charge was framed under Section 302/149 IPC.
The Magistrate took cognizance and committed the case to the Court of Session at Meerut where the case got registered as Sessions Trial No.1190 of 2016 and 1191 of 2016.

In support of its case the prosecution has also produced seven witnesses of fact who are identified as PW-1 to PW-7.
7.
P.W.-1 is the informant.
PW-2 is Shaudan Singh, who happens to be brother-in-law of the informant.
PW-3 is Vinod, who is the other brother-in-law of the informant.
PW-4 Yashpal Singh is the cousin of the deceased, who had received telephonic call with regard to illness of the deceased.
PW-5 Gajraj Singh is the uncle of the deceased.
PW-6 Dushyant is also uncle of the deceased.
PW-7 is the mother of the deceased.
All the witnesses of fact in the present case have turned hostile at the stage of examination-in-chief itself.
All these witnesses have specifically stated that neither there was any demand of dowry, nor the deceased was harassed and no physical or mental torture was extended to the deceased.
These witnesses have stated that the deceased and her husband were living as husband and wife without any dispute between them.
These witnesses have also stated that the deceased was suffering from respiratory problem and she was being treated by the doctors.
All the witnesses of fact have denied the suggestion that on account of any subsequent compromise between the parties they are not supporting the prosecution case.
8. PW-8 is Dr. Navneet Kumar Yadav, who is the autopsy surgeon and has proved the postmortem report.

In the cross-examination, PW-8 has admitted that all postmortem injuries were on account of burning and there were neither any external injury on the body of the deceased, nor any injury was caused on the deceased on account of strangulation, etc., prior to the death.
9. PW-9 is the Circle Officer, who has conducted investigation in the matter and has also filed the chargesheet in the case which has been duly proved.

The defence has also produced two witnesses, namely Vipin Chaudhary (DW-1) and Jai Prakash (DW-2).

These witnesses of fact have stated that no dowry was taken at the time of marriage and that the deceased was suffering from illness and she could not be cured despite various treatment offered to her.
DW-2 has also stated that at the time of cremation none of the family members of the deceased was present.
He has also stated that cremation was done after waiting for several hours for the family members of the deceased.
11. The above evidence has been confronted to the accused for recording their statement under Section 313 Cr.P.C.
They have clearly stated that evidence led by the prosecution to support the charges levelled against them are false and that they have been implicated on account of conspiracy.
Accused husband has also stated that the deceased died on account of illness and that he had got her treated by the doctor prior to her death.
The statement of other accused under Section 313 Cr.P.C. is on similar lines.
12. The trial court relying upon the evidence led by the prosecution has come to the conclusion that the prosecution has succeeded in establishing the guilt of the accused beyond reasonable doubt.
Before proceeding further, we may refer to Paper No. 28A, which is the Viscera Report, wherein Organochloro Insecticide Poison has been found in the viscera of the deceased.
The substance is found to be poisonous and the cause of death has been ascertained as poisoning.

14. The trial court has come to the conclusion that the conduct of the accused persons in setting up a false defence was a circumstance to discredit them and the mere fact that witnesses of fact have turned hostile would not be sufficient to hold the accused persons innocent in the matter.
Thus aggrieved, the accused persons are before this Court.

15. Sri Shad Khan, learned Advocate appearing for the appellants contends that since all prosecution witnesses of fact have turned hostile, as such, the finding of guilt of accused and subsequent conviction and sentence recorded by the trial court is erroneous and perverse.

He further submits that prosecution has not been able to establish that the deceased was poisoned by any of the accused and the possibility of deceased having consumed insecticide cannot be ruled out, particularly as the prosecution witnesses of fact have specifically asserted that she was suffering from respiratory disease.

Learned Advocate further submits that the prosecution having failed to prove necessary Kapil vs State Of U.P. on 6 November, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/106390973/
5 facts indicating existence of special facts or circumstances within the knowledge of the accused the prosecution cannot take advantage of Section 106 of the Evidence Act, nor the court below is justified in recording conviction and sentence of the accused appellants on such count.
Learned Advocate submits that this is a case of circumstantial evidence in which chain of circumstances is not complete.

He further submits that the alternative hypothesis consistent with the innocence of the accused cannot be ruled out, inasmuch as, the possibility of deceased having herself consumed poison cannot be entirely discarded.

He also submits that the possibility of accused persons not even knowing the fact that the deceased had consumed poison cannot be entirely eliminated and their statement that the deceased had fallen sick cannot be construed as putting up a false defence.

Learned counsel lastly submits that the viscera report on the basis of which poisoning is alleged has not been specifically confronted to the accused in his statement under Section 313 Cr.P.C. and,
therefore, such report cannot be read or relied upon against the accused appellants.

16. Sri Vikas Goswami (AGA-I) as well as Sri Rajesh Kumar Madheshia (brief holder) for the State on the other hand submits that the prosecution has clearly established the fact of it being a case of unnatural death of the deceased within the matrimonial house.
He submits that what happened in the secrecy of the house is not expected to be proved by the prosecution.
Learned AGA submits that the family members including the husband had the onus to explain such special circumstances which otherwise could be within the knowledge of the accused alone.

Learned AGA further submits that the conduct of the accused in cremating the body even before arrival of the family members as well as putting up a false defence of sickness of deceased are sufficient circumstances to connect the chain of circumstances required to be raised by the prosecution so as to prove the hypothesis of guilt specifically attributed to the accused and, therefore, the appeals lacks merit and are liable to be dismissed.

17. We have heard Sri Shad Khan, learned counsel for the appellants, Sri Vikas Goswami, learned A.G.A.-I as well as Sri Rajesh Kumar Madheshia for the State and have carefully perused the materials on record.
18. In the facts of the case, we find that the deceased died on account of poisoning.

This fact is clearly established from Paper No. 28A, which is the report of the Forensic Science Laboratory,
Agra, U.P., according to which, Organochloro Insecticide Poison was found in the viscera preserved of the deceased.
The postmortem report otherwise shows that cause of death was not ascertained and there were no anti-mortem injuries found on the body of the deceased.
The injury in the nature of burns on various parts of the body was postmortem injury and could not have been the cause of death.
It is also admitted on record that the deceased had died in her matrimonial house.
The date of death of the deceased is 24th March, 2016.
It is also admitted on record that on the very date of death of the deceased her body was put on pyre at the burning ghat (crematorium).

It is also admitted that on the arrival of PW-2 and PW-3 at the burning ghat the half burnt body of the deceased was taken out of the pyre and later inquest was conducted and postmortem was performed on partially burnt body of the deceased.
19.
The prosecution has charged the accused persons of demand of dowry as well as harassment meted out to her on account of non-fulfillment of such demand.

sentences.text: The charges against the accused persons under Section 3/4 of the Dowry Prohibition Act as well as under Section 498A/201/304B IPC have not been found proved by the Court of Session.
The trial court has convicted and sentenced the accused appellants under the alternative charges framed under Section 302/149 as well as 201/511 IPC.
In support of such charge there is no testimony of any of the prosecution witnesses of fact.

The prosecution case, therefore, survives only on the plea that the deceased died on account of poisoning inside her matrimonial house and that onus of the accused under Section 106 of the Evidence Act has not been discharged.
The prosecution also relies upon the fact that a false defence of illness was taken by the accused persons.
The evidence in that regard has been carefully perused by us and various submissions advanced by learned counsel for the parties with reference to the evidence on record has been considered.
20. First and foremost, we may note that the solitary evidence of prosecution to prove that the death had occurred on account of poisoning is the FSL report (Paper No. 28A).

This document has not been confronted to any of the accused for recording their statement under Section 313 Cr.P.C. Law is settled that unless an evidence is specifically confronted to the accused for securing his explanation such evidence cannot be taken into consideration.
21.
In addition to the fact that primary evidence i.e. the viscera report has not been confronted to accused, there are other reasons on record due to which the prosecution case cannot succeed.
Admittedly, the poison consumed by the deceased is organochloro which is used as an insecticide.

The deceased was married in an agricultural family and was residing in a village. Presence of insecticide in the house of a farming family is normal and no exception can be taken to presence of such insecticide in the house.
What has to be proved is that the deceased had herself not consumed the insecticide and that she was administered insecticide by the accused persons.
The evidence on record clearly shows that there was neither any motive for the accused persons to commit the offence, nor there was any demand of dowry.
The prosecution has not been able to place on record any evidence which may go to show that the deceased was administered poison by any of the accused persons.
Unless the prosecution is able to demonstrate that the deceased was administered poisoning by the accused persons the offence under Section 302 IPC cannot be proved.

22. Learned AGA has placed reliance upon the judgment of the Supreme Court in Trimukh Maroti Kirkan vs State Of Maharashtra, (2006) 10 SCC 681 as well as State of Punjab Vs. Karnail Singh (2003) 11 SCC 271 in order to submit that the unrealistic responsibility cannot be imposed upon the prosecution to prove the fact which may have occurred inside the secrecy of the house.

wherein the Court in paragraph 35 to 48 has held that the primary facts to attract the presumption under Section 106 of the Evidence Act will have to be proved by the prosecution before onus shifts Kapil vs State Of U.P. on 6 November, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/106390973/

sentences.text: The Supreme Court has taken note of the judgment in the case of Trimukh Maroti Kirkan (supra) for arriving at such conclusion.

The Court has clearly held that Section 106 of the Evidence Act is an exception to Section 101 of the Evidence Act, which lays down the general rule that in a criminal case the burden of proof is on the prosecution, and Section 106 of the Evidence Act is certainly not intended to relieve it of that duty. Paragraphs 43 to 46 of the judgment are relevant,
which are reproduced hereinafter:-
"43.
Thus, from the aforesaid decisions of this Court, it is evident that the court should apply Section 106 of the Evidence Act in criminal cases with care and caution.
It cannot be said that it has no application to criminal cases.

The ordinary rule which applies to criminal trials in this country that the onus lies on the prosecution to prove the guilt of the accused is not in any way modified by the provisions contained in Section 106 of the Evidence Act.
44. Section 106 of the Evidence Act cannot be invoked to make up the inability of the prosecution to produce evidence of circumstances pointing to the guilt of the accused.
This section cannot be used to support a conviction unless the prosecution has discharged the onus by proving all the elements necessary to establish the offence.

It does not absolve the prosecution from the duty of proving that a crime was committed even though it is a matter specifically within the knowledge of the accused and it does not throw the burden on the accused to show that no crime was committed.

To infer the guilt of the accused from absence of reasonable explanation in a case where the other circumstances are not by themselves enough to call for his explanation is to relieve the prosecution of its legitimate burden.
So, until a prima facie case is established by such evidence, the onus does not shift to the accused.

45. Section 106 of the Evidence Act obviously refers to cases where the guilt of the accused is established on the evidence produced by the prosecution unless the accused is able to prove some other facts especially within his knowledge, which would render the evidence of the prosecution nugatory.

If in such a situation, the accused offers an explanation which may be reasonably true in the proved circumstances, the accused gets the benefit of reasonable doubt though he may not be able to prove beyond reasonable doubt the truth of the explanation.
But, if the accused in such a case does not give any explanation at all or gives a false or unacceptable explanation, this by itself is a circumstance which may well turn the scale against him.

In the language of Prof. Glanville Williams:
"All that the shifting of the evidential burden does at the final stage of the case is to allow the jury (Court) to take into account the silence of the accused or the absence of satisfactory explanation appearing from his evidence."
(Emphasis supplied)

Kapil vs State Of U.P. on 6 November, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/106390973/
8 46.

To recapitulate the foregoing : What lies at the bottom of the various rules shifting the evidential burden or burden of introducing evidence in proof of one's case as opposed to the persuasive burden or burden of proof, i.e., of proving all the issues remaining with the prosecution and which never shift is the idea that it is impossible for the prosecution to give wholly convincing evidence on certain issues from its own hand and it is, therefore, for the accused to give evidence on them if he wishes to escape.
Positive facts must always be proved by the prosecution.
But the same rule cannot always apply to negative facts.
It is not for the prosecution to anticipate and eliminate all possible defences or circumstances which may exonerate an accused.

Again, when a person does not act with some intention other than that which the character and circumstances of the act suggest, it is not for the prosecution to eliminate all the other possible intentions.

If the accused had a different intention that is a fact especially within his knowledge and which he must prove (see Professor Glanville Williams-Proof of Guilt, Ch. 7, page 127 and following) and the interesting discussion-para 527 negative averments and para 528 - "require affirmative counter-evidence" at page 438 and foil, of Kenny's outlines of Criminal Law, 17th Edn. 1958."

24. Adverting to the facts of the present case, we have to see as to whether the prosecution has succeeded in establishing the fact that the deceased was administered poison by the accused persons or not?
Mere fact that poison was found in the viscera report would indicate that the deceased had consumed insecticide and it was the cause of her death.
Whether consumption of insecticide was forced upon the deceased or it was voluntary act of the deceased are two distinct eventualities which may arise in a case of poisoning.
There is nothing on record to show that the deceased was administered poisoning by the accused persons.
The possibility of deceased having consumed poison, herself, is an eventuality which cannot be brushed aside.
In the event the deceased had consumed insecticide on her own it is also possible that the family members may not have come to know of such fact.
What family members saw was that the deceased had suddenly fallen sick as she started vomiting and this fact alone was informed to the family members of the deceased.

In the absence of any evidence led by the prosecution to eliminate the possibility of such exigency of voluntary consumption of poison by the deceased, we would not be justified in placing the burden on the accused of explaining the circumstances in which the poison was consumed by the deceased with the aid of Section 106 of the Evidence Act.

The prosecution will have to show that it was within the knowledge of the accused that the deceased was administered poison or that she died on account of poisoning before we can place burden of Section 106 of the Evidence Act against the accused.

In the facts of the present case, we are thus of the view that the alternative hypothesis consistent with the innocence of the accused does exist as the deceased may have consumed insecticide to commit suicide.
In such exigency, the knowledge of poisoning as being the cause of sickness of the deceased cannot be imputed upon the family members.

In the absence of prosecution having proved the essential facts to attract the burden of Section 106 of the Evidence Act, the trial court was not justified in taking shelter of it so as to convict and sentence the accused appellants.

25. We may also refer to the judgment of the Supreme Court in Sharad Birdhichand Sarda Vs. State of Maharashtra, 1984 (4) SCC 116, which is a locus classicus on the circumstantial evidence wherein the court has dealt with the mode and manner of proving case of murder by administering poison.

sentences.text: We then pass on to another important point which seems to have been completely missed by the High Court.

It is well settled that where on the evidence two possibilities are available or open, one which goes in favour of the prosecution and the other which benefits an accused, the accused is undoubtedly entitled to the benefit of doubt.

In Kali Ram v. State of Himachal Pradesh,(l) this Court made the following observations:
"Another golden thread which runs through the web of the administration of justice in criminal cases is that if two views are possible on the evidence adduced in the case one pointing to the guilt of the accused and the other to his innocence, the view which is favourable to the accused should be adopted

sentences.text:
This principle has a special relevance in cases where in the guilt of the accused is sought to be established by circumstantial evidence."
163.
We now come to the mode and manner of proof of cases of murder by administration of poison.

In Ramgopal's case (supra) this Court held thus:
"Three questions arise in such cases, namely (firstly), did the deceased die of the poison in question ? (secondly), had the accused the poison in his possession ? and (thirdly), had the accused an opportunity to administer the poison in question to the deceased ?

It is only when the motive is there and these facts are all proved that the court may be able to draw the inference, that the poison was administered by the accused to the deceased resulting in his death."
164.

So far as this matter is concerned, in such cases the court must carefully scan the evidence and determine the four important circumstances which alone can justify a conviction:
(1) there is a clear motive for an accused to administer poison to the deceased, (2)
that the deceased died of poison said to have been administered, (3) that the accused had the poison in his possession, (4) that he had an opportunity to administer the poison to the deceased."
26.
In the facts of the present case except for the second exigency none of the other three exigencies enumerated in para 164 are shown to exist in the facts of the present case.
We moreover find that the prosecution evidence is not sufficient to connect the chain of circumstances which may lead to the hypothesis of guilt, specifically attributed to the accused appellants.
Unless the prosecution is able to do so the case based on circumstantial evidence cannot succeed.

The requisite conditions on fulfillment of which alone a case of circumstantial evidence be proved has been enumerated in para 152 and 153 of the judgment in Sharad Birdhichand Sarda (supra), which are reproduced hereinafter:-
"152.

A close analysis of this decision would show that the following conditions must be fulfilled before a case against an accused can be said to be fully established:

sentences.text: (1) the circumstances from which the conclusion of guilt is to be drawn should be fully established.

It may be noted here that this Court indicated that the circumstances concerned 'must or should'
and not 'may be' established.

There is not only a grammatical but a legal distinction between 'may be proved' and 'must be or should be proved' as was held by this Court in Shivaji Sahabrao Bobade &
Anr. v. State of Maharashtra(') where the following observations were made:
"Certainly, it is a primary principle that the accused must be and not merely may be guilty before a court can convict and the mental distance between 'may be' and 'must be' is long and divides vague conjectures from sure conclusions."

(2) The facts so established should be consistent only with the hypothesis of the guilt of the accused,
that is to say.
they should not be explainable on any other hypothesis except that the accused is guilty, (3) the circumstances should be of a conclusive nature and tendency.

(4) they should exclude every possible hypothesis except the one to be proved, and (5) there must be a chain of evidence so complete as not to leave any reasonable ground for the conclusion consistent with the innocence of the accused and must show that in all human probability the act must have been done by the accused.
153. These five golden principles, if we may say so, constitute the panchsheel of the proof of a case based on circumstantial evidence."
27.
In the facts of the case, we find that five golden principles evolved by the Supreme Court in Sharad Birdhichand (supra) are not shown to be attracted in the facts of the present case.
Not only that the chain of event is incomplete but the possible hypothesis consistent with the innocence of the accused also cannot be discounted.
Once that be so, we find that the conclusion drawn by the Court of Session to hold the accused appellants guilty of the offence under Section 302/149 IPC cannot be proved.
Even otherwise there is not even an iota of evidence to show that there was any prior meeting of mind and the applicability of Section 149 IPC is clearly shown to be missing.
There is no evidence to prove common object of the accused persons to commit murder of the deceased.
28. In that view of the matter, the conclusion and finding returned by the Court of Session based upon the evidence placed on record cannot be sustained.
We have gone through the judgment of the trial court which indicates that strong suspicion against the accused is the basis of his implication.

Law is settled that suspicion howsoever grave cannot be a substitute for positive evidence, which alone is required to be proved by the prosecution in order to establish the guilt of the accused persons.
29. In that view of the matter, we cannot subscribe to the conclusions and findings of the trial court which are accordingly reversed.
The present appeals succeed and are allowed.

The postmortem report otherwise shows that cause of death was not ascertained and there were no anti-mortem injuries found on the body of the deceased.
The injury in the nature of burns on various parts of the body was postmortem injury and could not have been the cause of death.
22. Learned AGA has placed reliance upon the judgment of the Supreme Court in Trimukh Maroti Kirkan vs State Of Maharashtra, (2006) 10 SCC 681 as well as State of Punjab Vs. Karnail Singh (2003) 11 SCC 271 in order to submit that the unrealistic responsibility cannot be imposed upon the prosecution to prove the fact which may have occurred inside the secrecy of the house.
opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
In support of such charge there is no testimony of any of the prosecution witnesses of fact.
The prosecution case, therefore, survives only on the plea that the deceased died on account of poisoning inside her matrimonial house and that onus of the accused under Section 106 of the Evidence Act has not been discharged.
This document has not been confronted to any of the accused for recording their statement under Section 313 Cr.P.C. Law is settled that unless an evidence is specifically confronted to the accused for securing his explanation such evidence cannot be taken into consideration.
21.
Admittedly, the poison consumed by the deceased is organochloro which is used as an insecticide.
The deceased was married in an agricultural family and was residing in a village. Presence of insecticide in the house of a farming family is normal and no exception can be taken to presence of such insecticide in the house.
What has to be proved is that the deceased had herself not consumed the insecticide and that she was administered insecticide by the accused persons.
The evidence on record clearly shows that there was neither any motive for the accused persons to commit the offence, nor there was any demand of dowry.
The prosecution has not been able to place on record any evidence which may go to show that the deceased was administered poison by any of the accused persons.
Unless the prosecution is able to demonstrate that the deceased was administered poisoning by the accused persons the offence under Section 302 IPC cannot be proved.
It is not for the prosecution to anticipate and eliminate all possible defences or circumstances which may exonerate an accused.
Again, when a person does not act with some intention other than that which the character and circumstances of the act suggest, it is not for the prosecution to eliminate all the other possible intentions.
Mere fact that poison was found in the viscera report would indicate that the deceased had consumed insecticide and it was the cause of her death.
Whether consumption of insecticide was forced upon the deceased or it was voluntary act of the deceased are two distinct eventualities which may arise in a case of poisoning.
There is nothing on record to show that the deceased was administered poisoning by the accused persons.
The possibility of deceased having consumed poison, herself, is an eventuality which cannot be brushed aside.
In the event the deceased had consumed insecticide on her own it is also possible that the family members may not have come to know of such fact.
What family members saw was that the deceased had suddenly fallen sick as she started vomiting and this fact alone was informed to the family members of the deceased.
In the absence of any evidence led by the prosecution to eliminate the possibility of such exigency of voluntary consumption of poison by the deceased, we would not be justified in placing the burden on the accused of explaining the circumstances in which the poison was consumed by the deceased with the aid of Section 106 of the Evidence Act.
The prosecution will have to show that it was within the knowledge of the accused that the deceased was administered poison or that she died on account of poisoning before we can place burden of Section 106 of the Evidence Act against the accused.
In the facts of the present case, we are thus of the view that the alternative hypothesis consistent with the innocence of the accused does exist as the deceased may have consumed insecticide to commit suicide.
In such exigency, the knowledge of poisoning as being the cause of sickness of the deceased cannot be imputed upon the family members.
In the absence of prosecution having proved the essential facts to attract the burden of Section 106 of the Evidence Act, the trial court was not justified in taking shelter of it so as to convict and sentence the accused appellants.
Not only that the chain of event is incomplete but the possible hypothesis consistent with the innocence of the accused also cannot be discounted.
Once that be so, we find that the conclusion drawn by the Court of Session to hold the accused appellants guilty of the offence under Section 302/149 IPC cannot be proved.
Even otherwise there is not even an iota of evidence to show that there was any prior meeting of mind and the applicability of Section 149 IPC is clearly shown to be missing.
There is no evidence to prove common object of the accused persons to commit murder of the deceased.
28. In that view of the matter, the conclusion and finding returned by the Court of Session based upon the evidence placed on record cannot be sustained.
Law is settled that suspicion howsoever grave cannot be a substitute for positive evidence, which alone is required to be proved by the prosecution in order to establish the guilt of the accused persons.
